Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
With a PCL-5 score of 39 charting her symptom load, Marisol had always known the river, but the autumn flood turned it into something unrecognizable. She was standing on her porch when the levee groaned, a sound that split the air like a cracking rib. Within hours, the water rose with a steady, heavy presence, swallowing streets and pooling against doorframes. What frightened her most was the sudden rush of air and the way the current pulled at the trees, sending branches scraping against her roof with a sharp, clatter. When the rescue boat pulled up, a worker called out to a neighbor named Elena, and Marisol felt a familiar tightness in her stomach, a wave of nausea that rose without warning. That night, as the wind howled and the water pressed against the windows, she felt certain that the river was still inside the house, even after the pumps began their rhythmic clicking. Over the following months, her days narrowed into a careful routine. She found herself avoiding going out, staying within the four walls of her living room where the floorboards felt solid and predictable. When the refrigerator hummed too loudly or a car backfired down the street, her shoulders tightened. She would deliberately try to leave her body, floating above the cushions while the noise continued. She had come to believe that stepping outside meant inviting the rising water back in, and so her world shrank to a handful of familiar rooms. Nights grew difficult; she lay awake, listening for any sudden shift in the air, her eyes fixed on the ceiling until dawn. What she missed most was the rhythm of her own life, and she found herself dwelling on how she used to be—how she used to walk the neighborhood, how she used to laugh without checking the sky first. Her work as a physical therapist did not disappear, but it adapted to her boundaries. She kept her clinic on the second floor of a brick building near the creek, where the large windows overlooked the same river that had risen. When a patient’s wheelchair rolled over the threshold or the hydrotherapy pool bubbled behind the glass, the sight of water would sometimes bring a quiet wave of nausea. Marisol would pause her demonstration, close her eyes, and let the sensation pass. Her memories of the flood did not arrive as clear pictures. Sometimes, she would feel the full emotional intensity of that night without any image at all, a sudden pressure in her chest that made her hand drift to her throat. Other times, when she heard the names of those who had been on the evacuation list, the sound would pull the event into focus, heavy with grief. She had come to understand that the memory felt alien, as if it belonged to a woman who had stood on that porch, yet it was undeniably hers. The clinic, the home, the sound of the pumps—all coexisted in her quiet days. It was the quiet accumulation of these moments that finally brought her to therapy. She had stopped answering the phone when she knew it was the community center, worried that a loud voice on the line would startle her back into the rising water. She was most afraid of losing her safe zone, of the narrow circle of familiar places widening into a world of unpredictable sounds and rising tides. What she hoped for was not to forget, but to recognize the boundary between then and now, to feel the nausea, the sound, the name, and simply stand firm when the river was only water.
